chunks: As for what Muhammad b. Ya'qub narrated from 'Ali b. Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad b. Abi 'Umayr and Muhammad b. Isma'il from al-Fadl b. Shadhan — all of them from Hammad b. 'Isa, from Hariz, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him):

He said: When the water is more than a rawiya, nothing shall make it impure — whether something decomposes in it or does not decompose in it — unless a smell comes upon it that overpowers the smell of the water.

This does not contradict what we have previously presented of narrations, because he said 'when the water is more than a rawiya,' making clear that it carries no impurity only when it exceeds the rawiya; and it is not excluded that what is meant by that excess is the amount by which the kurr is completed.

key_terms.الْكُرِّ: kurr — the minimum volume of water that cannot be rendered ritually impure; a key measure in Shia fiqh
key_terms.تَفَسَّخَ: tafassakh — to decompose or disintegrate (of a body or substance dissolving in water)
key_terms.رَاوِيَةٍ: rawiya — a large water vessel (approximately one camel-load of water), used here as a jurisprudential volume threshold

ai.seo_question: What volume of water cannot be made ritually impure according to Imam al-Baqir (AS) in al-Istibsar?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) rules that water exceeding the measure of a rawiya (a large vessel) cannot be rendered ritually impure by anything dissolved or decomposing within it, unless an odor arising from that matter overpowers the smell of the water itself. Al-Shaykh al-Tusi then reconciles this narration with previously cited reports, arguing that the 'excess beyond a rawiya' corresponds precisely to the additional volume needed to complete the kurr — the standard minimum of uncontaminatable water in Shia fiqh.
